Module io.github.brantunger.unruly.core
Package io.github.brantunger.unruly.api.language

Class FactProperties

java.lang.Object
io.github.brantunger.unruly.api.language.FactProperties
public final class FactProperties extends Object
Reads a property of a fact the way rules expect: a record component, a JavaBean getter or a Map key.

Rules everywhere are written applicant.creditScore, where the fact may be a record, a bean or a map. The engine hands a language the fact objects as they are, so making that work is each language's job, and every language that does it by hand does it slightly differently: one reads a record's component as a method and silently evaluates the condition to false, another fails only for records, a third converts every fact to a map on every evaluation. A language may use this instead.

Writing a property is the other direction, and the engine already has it: OutputWriter.beansAndMaps() puts into a map or calls a bean setter. There is deliberately no write here, so there's only one implementation to keep correct. Records can't be written to at all.

Accessors are looked up once for each class and shared by every thread.

  • Method Details

    • read

      public static @Nullable Object read(Object target, String property)
      Reads a property of a fact.
      • A Map: the value under that exact key. A key that isn't there is an error, and a key whose value is null isn't. A map whose keys aren't strings has no property a rule can name, even though toData(java.lang.Object, int) gives those keys a string form.
      • A record: the component of that name, or one of its own getters when no component matches.
      • Anything else: the public no-argument getProperty(), or isProperty() when it returns a boolean or a Boolean. A class declaring both resolves to getProperty(), so the choice never depends on the order reflection reports methods in. Public fields aren't read.

      A fact whose own class isn't public is read through a public type above it that declares the accessor, which is what makes a fact from a factory, or an anonymous implementation of a public interface, readable. When nothing public declares it, the accessor is called directly if the class's package is open to this module: every package on the class path is, and on the module path the application opens it with opens. Exporting the package isn't enough, because calling a method of a class that isn't public is deep reflection.

      Parameters:
      target - The fact, which must not be null
      property - The property's name, as the rule wrote it
      Returns:
      The property's value, which may be null
      Throws:
      NullPointerException - if target or property is null
      IllegalArgumentException - if the fact has no such property. A language should let this reach the engine, which fails the rule with it: a missing property is a mistake in the rule, and evaluating it to false or to undefined hides it
      IllegalStateException - if the property exists but can't be read, because nothing public declares its accessor and its package isn't open to this module; or if the accessor threw, with what it threw as the cause. What an accessor throws is always wrapped, so that a getter throwing IllegalArgumentException isn't read as a missing property

    • toData

      public static Map<String,@Nullable Object> toData(Object target, int depth)
      Converts a record, a bean or a map into a map of its properties, for a language that reads only maps.

      Every step down costs one level, whether it's into a property, into a map's value or into a collection's element. At 1 the values are whatever the properties hold; at 2 a value that is itself convertible becomes a map, and a list becomes a list of the elements as they are; at 3 the elements of that list are converted too.

      A value already being converted higher up the same path is left as it is rather than converted again, so a fact that holds itself, or two facts that hold each other, cost no more than a tree of the same depth. That stops a value repeating down one path; it doesn't make every graph cheap. A value reachable by several different paths is converted once for each of them, so an object graph that fans out and rejoins can still cost far more than it holds. depth is what bounds that, and it's chosen by the caller, not by the facts: convert as few levels as the language needs.

      A map's values keep their keys, with a key that isn't a String converted by String.valueOf(java.lang.Object). Two keys that read the same then collapse into one entry and the later wins, and a null key becomes the entry "null", which a real "null" key can't be told apart from. read(java.lang.Object, java.lang.String) takes the key as it is, so a converted map can show a property that reading the fact directly can't reach.

      A value is converted when it's a map, a collection, an array of objects, a record, or an application class with at least one getter. Everything the JVM itself provides is left as it is, which is what keeps a String, a Path, a LocalDate, an Optional, an enum, a lambda or an array of primitives from being taken apart into the properties of its implementation. A proxy over an interface is data, because that's a shape facts take: a projection, a lazy association, a test double. A lambda or an anonymous class is converted when it's the target, because then the caller asked for its properties, and left alone when it's met as a value.

      The rule is "has getters", so it can't tell data from a library type that merely looks like it. A JSON tree node or a multimap from a third-party library has isEmpty(), isArray() and the like, so converting a fact that holds one returns those flags instead of its contents. Read such a fact with read(java.lang.Object, java.lang.String), or have the language convert it itself.

      Parameters:
      target - The record, bean or map to convert, which must not be null
      depth - How many levels to convert, from 1 to 20
      Returns:
      The properties by name: a record's components in the order it declares them, then any other getters it has, and a bean's sorted by name, because reflection reports a class's methods in no particular order. A new modifiable map
      Throws:
      NullPointerException - if target is null
      IllegalArgumentException - if depth is outside 1 to 20, or target is a value this doesn't take apart, such as a String, a number or a collection
      IllegalStateException - if an accessor can't be called, with what it threw as the cause
